leads.text: In lib/handler/redirect-handler.js, shouldRemoveHeader() strips cross-origin-sensitive request headers using a LENGTH GATE `header.length === 13 || header.length === 6`, which only ever matches 'authorization' (13 chars) and 'cookie' (6 chars). 'proxy-authorization' is 19 characters, so it NEVER matches and is forwarded verbatim to the new origin after a cross-origin redirect. Attacker-controlled input is the Location response header from the upstream server (returned by parseLocation() at line 184-195 from the raw `headers[i+1]`), which is parsed into a new origin at line 113 and then re-dispatched at line 171 with the uncleaned headers assigned at line 119. The same library's fetch path does strip it, proving intent: lib/web/fetch/index.js lines 1326/1329/1332/1333 delete 'authorization', 'proxy-authorization', 'cookie' AND 'host' on !sameOrigin. Reachable path: RedirectHandler.onHeaders (reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=2) -> cleanRequestHeaders (line 212) -> shouldRemoveHeader (line 197). A malicious or compromised HTTP server can return a 302 to its own origin and harvest the caller's proxy credentials.
leads.evidence: Query 1: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE toLower(c.code) CONTAINS 'proxy-authorization' ... -> returned lib/web/fetch/index.js:1329 `request.headersList.delete('proxy-authorization', true)` (reach=true) but NO such delete anywhere in lib/handler/ or lib/interceptor/. Query 2: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE (c.file_path STARTS WITH 'lib/handler/' OR c.file_path STARTS WITH 'lib/interceptor/') AND (c.code CONTAINS 'proxy' OR c.code CONTAINS 'Proxy' OR c.code CONTAINS 'cleanRequestHeaders' OR c.code CONTAINS 'shouldRemoveHeader') -> 8 rows, ZERO containing 'proxy'; only line 119 `this.opts.headers = cleanRequestHeaders(this.opts.headers, statusCode === 303, this.opts.origin !== origin)`, line 197 shouldRemoveHeader def, line 212 cleanRequestHeaders def, lines 216/222 call sites. Query 3 (sink lines in fetch strip block): MATCH (c:CpgCall...) WHERE c.file_path='lib/web/fetch/index.js' AND c.line>=1290 AND c.line<=1360 -> 1324 `sameOrigin(requestCurrentURL(request), locationURL)`, 1326 delete 'authorization', 1329 delete 'proxy-authorization', 1332 delete 'cookie', 1333 delete 'host' (all reach=true). Query 4 (reachability): MATCH (m:CpgMethod...) WHERE m.file_path='lib/handler/redirect-handler.js' -> shouldRemoveHeader line 197 reach=true hops=0; cleanRequestHeaders line 212 reach=true hops=0; RedirectHandler:onHeaders line 90 reach=true hops=2. semantic_search returned the verbatim source of shouldRemoveHeader confirming the `header.length === 13 || header.length === 6` gate and that only 'authorization'/'cookie' are returned.

leads.text: In lib/web/cookies/util.js, validateCookieDomain() (lines 124-132) validates ONLY that the domain does not start with '-' or end with '.' or '-'. It does not reject 0x3B (';'), ',' or control characters. stringify() then interpolates the value directly into the Set-Cookie header via `out.push(`Domain=${cookie.domain}`)` (line 249), which is joined and passed to headers.append('Set-Cookie', str) at lib/web/cookies/index.js:105. The 'domain' field is declared as a bare webidl.converters.DOMString in webidl.converters.Cookie (lib/web/cookies/index.js), so no character constraint is applied upstream either. This is an asymmetry with the sibling validator: validateCookiePath() (lines 105-117) DOES reject code 0x3B (';'), CTLs (<0x20) and 0x7F. Consequently an application calling setCookie(headers, {name, value, domain: untrustedInput}) lets an attacker inject additional Set-Cookie attributes (e.g. domain = 'example.com; Path=/; SameSite=None'). Note honestly: full CRLF response splitting is blocked downstream by isValidHeaderValue() (lib/web/fetch/util.js:156-176, rejects \r, \n, \0), so the primitive is attribute injection rather than header splitting, and duplicate-attribute precedence limits impact because the injected text is emitted before the legitimate Path/Expires/SameSite entries in `out`.
leads.evidence: semantic_search 'validateCookiePath validateCookieDomain validateCookieValue throw on invalid characters' returned verbatim source: `function validateCookieDomain (domain) { if (domain.startsWith('-') || domain.endsWith('.') || domain.endsWith('-')) { throw new Error('Invalid cookie domain') } }` (lib/web/cookies/util.js:124-132) vs `function validateCookiePath (path) { ... if (code < 0x20 || code === 0x7F || code === 0x3B) { throw new Error('Invalid cookie path') } }` (lines 105-117). Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall {scan_id:$scan_id}) WHERE c.file_path='lib/web/cookies/util.js' AND c.line>=200 AND c.line<=275 -> line 217 validateCookieName(cookie.name), 218 validateCookieValue(cookie.value), 220 formatString(cookie.name,'=',cookie.value), 243 validateCookieMaxAge, 248 validateCookieDomain(cookie.domain), 249 push(`Domain=${cookie.domain}`), 253 validateCookiePath, 254 push(`Path=${cookie.path}`). Query: MATCH (c:CpgCall...) WHERE c.code CONTAINS 'cookie' ... -> lib/web/cookies/index.js:100 `webidl.converters.Cookie(cookie)` (reach=true), :102 `stringify(cookie)` (reach=true), :105 `headers.append('Set-Cookie', str)` (reach=true). semantic_search on the Cookie converter confirmed `{converter: webidl.nullableConverter(webidl.converters.DOMString), key: 'domain', defaultValue: null}` with no allowedValues, while sameSite has `allowedValues: ['Strict','Lax','None']`. Method reachability: validateCookieDomain line 124 reach=true hops=0; stringify line 212 reach=true hops=0.

leads.text: MISSING PROTOTYPE GUARD on the response-header accumulator in `parseHeaders`. At lib/core/util.js:249 the accumulator is created as a prototype-inheriting plain object (`if (obj === undefined) obj = {}`), with no `Object.create(null)` / `{__proto__: null}` / `Object.hasOwn` guard — even though this same codebase applies exactly that control to its other header lookup tables (`Object.setPrototypeOf(headerNameLowerCasedRecord, null)` at lib/core/constants.js:113 and `Object.setPrototypeOf(normalizeMethodRecord, null)` at lib/web/fetch/util.js:746-747). Because `key` at line 251 is a SERVER-CONTROLLED response header name (lowercased via `headerNameToString`), a response header whose name collides with an `Object.prototype` member (`constructor`, `toString`, `valueOf`, `hasOwnProperty`, `isPrototypeOf`, `propertyIsEnumerable`, `__defineGetter__`, `__proto__`, ...) makes `let val = obj[key]` (line 252) resolve to an inherited function/object instead of `undefined`. `if (val)` is then truthy, `typeof val === 'string'` is false, so the `val = [val]` normalization at line 256 is skipped and line 259 executes `val.push(headers[i + 1].toString('utf8'))` on a non-array — `Object.push` / `Object.prototype.push` does not exist, throwing a TypeError inside response-header parsing. Same defect applies to the trailer accumulator passed at lib/api/api-request.js:127.

MISSING `proxy-authorization` STRIPPING on cross-origin redirect in the core dispatcher redirect path. `shouldRemoveHeader` (lib/handler/redirect-handler.js:197-209) removes only `authorization` and `cookie` when the redirect target origin differs, and it gates that removal behind a header-name-length fast path `unknownOrigin && (header.length === 13 || header.length === 6)` — `proxy-authorization` is 19 characters, so it can never be matched and is forwarded verbatim to the redirect target. The intended control demonstrably exists in this same repository on the fetch() path, which deletes all four credential headers (lib/web/fetch/index.js:1326 `authorization`, :1329 `proxy-authorization`, :1332 `cookie`, :1333 `host`) when `sameOrigin(requestCurrentURL(request), locationURL)` is false — proving the omission in redirect-handler.js is a gap, not a deliberate scope decision. Consequence: an app calling undici.request/stream/pipeline (or using Agent/Pool/RedirectHandler/the redirect interceptor) with `maxRedirections > 0` and a manually-set `proxy-authorization` header leaks that proxy credential to any attacker-controlled host named in a Location response header. Note ProxyAgent's `throwIfProxyAuthIsSent` (lib/dispatcher/proxy-agent.js:182-184) only blocks this header on the ProxyAgent.dispatch path, not on the plain request path that RedirectHandler serves.

NO CSPRNG AND NO BOUNDARY-COLLISION CHECK for the multipart/form-data delimiter. lib/web/fetch/body.js:103 builds the boundary as `----formdata-undici-0${`${Math.floor(Math.random() * 1e11)}`.padStart(11, '0')}` — `Math.random()` is a non-cryptographic PRNG (V8 xorshift128+, whose internal state is recoverable from a few observed outputs), so the delimiter is predictable rather than unguessable. Separately, nothing validates that serialized part content does not contain the delimiter: the only neutralization applied is `escape()` at line 108 (`str.replace(/
/g,'%0A').replace(//g,'%0D').replace(/"/g,'%22')`), which is applied ONLY to the field `name` (line 125, 130) and `filename` (line 131), while a string field's VALUE passes through `normalizeLinefeeds` at line 109 (`value.replace(/?
|/g, '
')`) which merely canonicalizes line endings and preserves `-`, so `--<boundary>` survives intact. A query for every call referencing `boundary` in lib/ returns no `includes`/`indexOf`/`test` collision check in body.js. Consequence: an attacker who can both supply a FormData field value and learn/predict one boundary (boundaries are emitted in the Content-Type header at line 167) can inject `
--<boundary>
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="..."

...` into the value and forge or override additional multipart parts seen by the receiving server.

leads.text:
DISABLED (STUBBED) CORS / CORP / TIMING-ALLOW-ORIGIN RESPONSE CHECKS in fetch. lib/web/fetch/util.js:220-234 defines three security checks as argument-ignoring stubs that unconditionally return the permissive verdict: `function crossOriginResourcePolicyCheck () { // TODO
 return 'allowed' }`, `function corsCheck () { // TODO
 return 'success' }`, and `function TAOCheck () { // TODO
 return 'success' }` — note each is declared with ZERO parameters, so the request/response passed by callers is discarded. These are not dead code: they are invoked on the live response path in `httpFetch` at lib/web/fetch/index.js:1160 `corsCheck(request, response) === 'failure'` (guarding `makeNetworkError('cors failure')` at :1162), :1167 `TAOCheck(request, response) === 'failure'`, and :1178 `crossOriginResourcePolicyCheck(request.origin, request.client, request.destination, actualResponse)` (guarding `makeNetworkError('blocked')` at :1185). Because the stubs can never return 'failure'/'blocked', those network errors are unreachable: a response is never validated against `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` or `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy`. Consequence: an application that sets `mode: 'cors'` on a fetch to a user-supplied or redirect-controlled URL and relies on undici to reject responses lacking a permissive `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` receives the cross-origin response body as if it had been authorized. `appendFetchMetadata` (util.js:237+) is likewise a partial stub, setting only `sec-fetch-mode` with `// TODO` for Sec-Fetch-Dest/Site/User.

`crossOriginResourcePolicyCheck()` in lib/web/fetch/util.js:220 is a disabled stub: body is `// TODO` then `return 'allowed'`, ignoring all four arguments it is called with. The live reachable guard at lib/web/fetch/index.js:1177-1178 is `if ((request.responseTainting === 'opaque' || response.type === 'opaque') && crossOriginResourcePolicyCheck(request.origin, request.client, request.destination, actualResponse) === 'blocked')`. Since the stub always returns 'allowed', the `=== 'blocked'` branch can never fire, so Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy is never enforced on opaque responses despite the call being present and passing four real arguments. Same upstream-stub caveat as corsCheck applies.

`tryUpgradeRequestToAPotentiallyTrustworthyURL(request)` in lib/web/fetch/util.js:679 has a completely empty body apart from a `// TODO` comment — it accepts a `request` parameter and does nothing with it. It is still called unconditionally from `mainFetch` at lib/web/fetch/index.js:531 (reachable_from_entry=true, hop_distance=1). This is the upgrade-insecure-requests protection: a request that should be rewritten from http: to https: is silently left on cleartext, so the mitigation is a no-op while the call site implies it is applied. Note lib/core/constants.js:91 still pushes the 'Upgrade-Insecure-Requests' header name, showing the feature is nominally present.

leads.text: `coarsenTime(timestamp, crossOriginIsolatedCapability)` in lib/web/fetch/util.js:307 is a disabled stub: body is `// TODO` then `return timestamp`, ignoring the `crossOriginIsolatedCapability` argument entirely. This function exists specifically to blunt high-resolution-timer side channels by clamping timestamp precision, and it is invoked six times on reachable paths (lib/web/fetch/util.js:326,327,328,329,330,337 — the resource-timing / markResourceTiming path), including on `performance.now()` at line 337. Every caller therefore receives full-precision, un-coarsened timing data, so the timing-attack mitigation is inert while appearing to be applied at every call site.

`TAOCheck()` in lib/web/fetch/util.js:232 is a disabled stub — `// TODO` then `return 'success'`, ignoring its arguments. The live reachable guard at lib/web/fetch/index.js:1167 is `TAOCheck(request, response) === 'failure'`, which can never evaluate true. The Timing-Allow-Origin check that is supposed to gate whether cross-origin timing detail is exposed is therefore never enforced, while the call site is written as though it gates something.

Inconsistent/partially-reverted TLS certificate verification across the benchmark harness: `rejectUnauthorized: false` is LIVE in benchmarks/benchmark.js:103-107, benchmarks/post-benchmark.js:115-119 and benchmarks/benchmark-http2.js:57-74 (two sites, including the global dispatcher via setGlobalDispatcher), but in benchmarks/benchmark-https.js the very same option has been COMMENTED OUT at four sites (lines 50, 61, 80, 91) leaving only `ca` and `servername`. That is the signature of a fix applied in one file and never propagated to its three siblings — someone disabled cert validation, then re-enabled it in exactly one place. Scope caveat for verifier: this is benchmark-only code, all six nodes report reachable_from_entry=false, and it is not part of the shipped library surface, so impact is limited to the dev/benchmark harness (MITM of benchmark traffic) rather than library consumers — hence LOW.

Quadratic ReDoS (catastrophic backtracking) in the regex LITERAL `/( )+$/` at lib/web/fetch/data-url.js:89, inside `dataURLProcessor`. The literal has an unanchored start with a `+`-quantified atom pinned to `$` — the classic O(n^2) shape: when no match exists, the engine retries from every space offset and backtracks the whole remaining run each time. It is applied to `mimeType`, which is taken from the attacker/caller-supplied `data:` URL: `URLSerializer(dataURL, true)` -> `.slice(5)` -> `collectASequenceOfCodePointsFast(',', ...)`, i.e. everything before the first comma, with no length bound. Step 6 of dataURLProcessor strips only LEADING and TRAILING whitespace, so an interior run of spaces survives. Line 89 is gated on line 71 (`/;( ){0,}base64$/i`) matching, which only requires the mimeType to END in `;base64` — it does not require the long space run to be near the end. Concrete input: `data:x<100000 spaces>y;base64,AAAA`. mimeType = `x` + 100000 spaces + `y;base64`; line 71 matches; line 85 `slice(0,-6)` yields `x`+100000 spaces+`y;`; line 89's regex then has NO possible match (string ends in `;`), so the engine pays ~n^2/2 ≈ 5e9 backtracking steps, hanging the event loop. Reached via fetch(): lib/web/fetch/index.js:922 `dataURLProcessor(currentURL)`, hop_distance 1. OPEN QUESTION the verifier must settle: whether the WHATWG URL serializer preserves literal U+0020 in a `data:` opaque path or percent-encodes it to %20 — if it percent-encodes, this is not exploitable via fetch() and only via any direct/other caller of dataURLProcessor. Note that undici's own line-71 literal explicitly tolerates spaces between `;` and `base64`, and line 89 exists solely to strip surviving spaces, which is in-data evidence that literal spaces do reach here.

Missing anchors in the validation regex LITERAL `HTTP_QUOTED_STRING_TOKENS = /[\u0009 -~\u0080-ÿ]/` at lib/web/fetch/data-url.js:16. The literal is a bare character class with no `^`/`$` anchors and no `+` quantifier, so `.test(s)` returns true if ANY SINGLE character of `s` is in the allowed set — not, as the MIME Sniffing spec requires, if `s` SOLELY consists of HTTP quoted-string token code points. Compare the sibling literal on line 10, `HTTP_TOKEN_CODEPOINTS = /^[...]+$/`, which IS correctly anchored — showing the author's intent was whole-string validation. It is used as the sole content gate for MIME-type parameter values at lib/web/fetch/data-url.js:419, inside the accept condition `parameterName.length !== 0 && HTTP_TOKEN_CODEPOINTS.test(parameterName) && (parameterValue.length === 0 || HTTP_QUOTED_STRING_TOKENS.test(parameterValue)) && !mimeType.parameters.has(parameterName)` (line 417), after which line 422 does `mimeType.parameters.set(parameterName, parameterValue)`. Consequence: a parameter value containing control characters (CR, LF, NUL, U+007F) passes validation as long as it contains at least one printable ASCII character — e.g. `a/b;p="x\r\nX-Injected: 1"` is accepted because the `x` matches. The tainted parameter map is then re-emitted by `serializeAMimeType` (lib/web/fetch/data-url.js:551), which escapes only `"` and `\` (line 575, `value.replace(/(\\|")/g, '\\$1')`) and NOT control characters, and that serialization becomes a Content-Type header value at lib/web/fetch/index.js:931 `serializeAMimeType(dataURLStruct.mimeType)` and at lib/web/fileapi/util.js:241 `serializeAMimeType(parsed)` (Blob.type normalization, where the input string is fully caller-controlled and unconstrained by any URL/header parser). Verifier should note there is a second line of defense for outgoing H1 headers — `headerCharRegex = /[^\t\x20-\x7e\x80-\xff]/` at lib/core/util.js:513 — which does reject CR/LF, so rank this as a validation/spec-conformance bypass (control chars in the U+0080-U+00FF and U+007F ranges still pass both) rather than a confirmed CRLF injection.

Known-vulnerable third-party component declared in the dependency manifest: `ws` at version range `^8.11.0`. The declared floor 8.11.0 is below 8.17.1, the release that fixes CVE-2024-37890 / GHSA-3h5v-q93c-6h6q — a denial of service in `ws` where a request with a very large number of HTTP headers crashes the receiving process (`Array.prototype.push` on an over-length header list). Any install that resolves to the floor of the `^8.11.0` range (an existing lockfile, `--prefer-offline`, a vendored cache, or a reproducible older build) ships the vulnerable code. This is the components-with-known-vulnerabilities class and does not depend on any request flow. Caveat the verifier should confirm from the manifest directly: the `:Dependency` nodes in this graph carry only {name, version, scan_id} with no dev/prod flag, and the surrounding set (jest, borp, c8, standard, tsd, husky, jsfuzz, proxy, https-pem, @matteo.collina/tspl) is clearly test/build tooling, so `ws` is most likely a devDependency used by undici's WebSocket test server — which lowers real-world impact to CI/test infrastructure rather than library consumers.

Known-vulnerable third-party component declared in the dependency manifest: `form-data` at version range `^4.0.0`. The declared floor 4.0.0 is below 4.0.4, the release that fixes CVE-2025-7783 / GHSA-fjxv-7rqg-78g4 — `form-data` used `Math.random()` to generate multipart boundary strings, making boundaries predictable and allowing an attacker who controls part of a form field value to forge boundary delimiters and inject additional multipart parts (parameter/part injection). Any install resolving to the floor of the `^4.0.0` range ships the vulnerable generator. Same caveat as the `ws` lead: the `:Dependency` nodes expose only {name, version, scan_id} with no dev/prod flag, and the surrounding manifest contents indicate this is test tooling (used alongside `formdata-node ^6.0.3` in undici's FormData tests), so impact is most likely confined to the test suite.

End-of-life / unmaintained third-party components declared in the dependency manifest (components-with-known-vulnerabilities class, no request flow required). From the 23 enumerated `:Dependency` nodes: (1) `@types/node ^18.0.3` — pins the typings to Node 18, which reached end-of-life in April 2025, so the project's declared type surface targets an unsupported, no-longer-security-patched runtime; (2) `jsdom ^24.0.0` — a superseded major (current line is 26/27); older jsdom majors drag in older transitive parsers (nwsapi, tough-cookie) that have carried their own advisories; (3) `pre-commit ^1.2.2` — abandoned since ~2016 and unmaintained, and it is redundant here because `husky ^9.0.7` is also declared, so the repo carries two git-hook managers one of which receives no security maintenance; (4) `jsfuzz ^1.0.15` — unmaintained fuzzing harness. Each of these is a maintenance/EOL exposure rather than a specific CVE; the verifier should resolve the actual installed tree (lockfile) and re-check each against an advisory database. Also confirmed NOT vulnerable on inspection of the same result set, and should not be flagged: `node-forge ^1.3.1` (1.3.0+ already fixes CVE-2022-24771/24772/24773) and `dns-packet ^5.4.0` (5.4.0 is itself the fix for CVE-2023-0842).

leads.text: Nested-quantifier regex LITERAL reachable from untrusted input: `/^127(?:\.[0-9]+){0,2}\.[0-9]+$|^\[(?:0*:)*?:?0*1\]$/` at lib/web/fetch/util.js:535, inside `isOriginPotentiallyTrustworthy` (nested in `isURLPotentiallyTrustworthy` at line 505), applied to `originAsURL.hostname`. The second alternative contains `(?:0*:)*?` — a quantifier nested directly inside another quantifier, the textbook catastrophic-backtracking signature this shape looks for, and the reason I am reporting it. I want to be explicit that my own manual analysis suggests it is probably NOT exponential in practice: each iteration of the inner group must consume exactly one literal `:`, which pins the iteration boundaries, so the number of iterations is fixed by the colon count and the greedy `0*` runs are non-overlapping — making the match linear. It is reported at LOW confidence so an independent verifier can settle it empirically rather than have it silently dropped, since the literal does match the dangerous syntactic pattern. Two mitigating factors the verifier should weigh: `originAsURL.hostname` comes from `new URL(origin)`, so the WHATWG URL parser has already normalized/validated any IPv6 literal before the regex sees it (bounding both length and alphabet), and both alternatives are fully `^`/`$` anchored, so there is only one start offset. The first alternative, `^127(?:\.[0-9]+){0,2}\.[0-9]+$`, has a `{0,2}`-bounded outer quantifier and so admits at most a constant number of split candidates.

Backtracking-prone regex LITERAL in the Subresource-Integrity parser: `const parseHashWithOptions = /(?<algo>sha256|sha384|sha512)-(?<hash>[A-Za-z0-9+\/]+={0,2}(?=\s|$))( +[!-~]*)?/i` at lib/web/fetch/util.js:627, executed at lib/web/fetch/util.js:649 as `parseHashWithOptions.exec(token)` inside `parseMetadata` (line 633, reachable_from_entry=true), where `token` iterates over `metadata.split(' ')` (line 644) and `metadata` is the caller-supplied `integrity` option, reaching here via lib/web/fetch/util.js:561 `parseMetadata(metadataList)`. The literal has the risky combination of an unbounded `[A-Za-z0-9+/]+`, an adjacent optional `={0,2}`, a following lookahead `(?=\s|$)` that can FAIL after the `+` has consumed a long run, and no `^`/`$` anchor on the overall pattern — so each candidate start offset can pay O(n) backtracking (e.g. token `sha256-` + `A`*n + `-` forces the `+` to give back every character). My own manual analysis suggests this stays roughly LINEAR overall rather than quadratic, because the required `sha256-`/`sha384-`/`sha512-` prefix needs a literal `-`, and `-` is absent from the `[A-Za-z0-9+/]` class, so the alnum runs belonging to different start offsets are disjoint and the per-offset costs sum to O(n). Reported at LOW confidence so a verifier can benchmark it rather than have the pattern silently dropped. Exploitability is further limited because `integrity` is set by the application calling fetch(), not by a remote peer.
